prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms are trapped at a magic wavelength so that many of them can be interrogated without Doppler, recoil or light-shift perturbation, bringing optical clocks to uncertainties near one part in 10^18

statement.case_for: I move my preferred configuration from B044 (magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene) to B018, the optical lattice clock, credited to Katori and Ye. The reason is the exchange in round 1 and the chair's questions, not the count of supporters. My own test is whether a result is robust, quantitatively understood and independently confirmed, and the lattice clock meets it more completely than any other candidate. Katori's magic-wavelength condition is a statement about atomic structure: at a chosen wavelength the light shifts of the two clock states cancel, so thousands of neutral atoms can be held in the Lamb-Dicke regime with no Doppler or recoil shift. That is a different physical idea from the frequency comb (2005), which counts optical cycles, and from the control of single trapped ions (2012), which gets stability from one quantum system. The lattice gets it from the statistics of a large ensemble while keeping single-particle systematic control. Many laboratories (Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE and others) have reproduced the performance on several species, and inter-laboratory comparisons check the uncertainty budgets, which is the independent confirmation I ask for. Millimetre-scale gravitational redshift and many-body clock physics are physical results about nature, so this is more than a performance record. Credit is two names, with the concept and first realisation to Katori and the accuracy, coherence and many-body clock work to Ye. The citation should state the magic-wavelength lattice and many-atom interrogation so the distinction from 2005 and 2012 is on the page.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes remains a real objection. If a colleague regards the clock as a better instrument rather than a new physical result, the novelty is smaller than for a new state of matter, and that was my own first reading. Ye's heritage in the Hall comb work means the citation must separate the lattice and accuracy contributions from comb infrastructure. The redefinition of the second has not happened, so some of the consequence is prospective. Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and the Yb and Hg groups contributed to the accuracy campaign and are outside two names. I am not an expert on clock metrology and cannot verify the current record uncertainties from the files, so I defer to the atomic physicists and to expert review on those numbers. Separately, I still think B044 is the discovery with the greater novelty in nature, and I accept that this trades maturity of the story and cleanliness of credit against novelty.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the magic-wavelength lattice is a new physical idea about light shifts and not a tuning of the earlier prizes, and asks me what in the twisted bilayer physical picture is settled enough to write into a citation.
responses.response: Her argument moved me on B018. The comb is a ruler and ion control is single-system control, whereas the magic-wavelength condition lets an ensemble be interrogated without perturbing the transition. I accept that as a distinct physical principle, provided the citation names it. Her question to me is also fair, and I cannot answer it fully. What is settled for B044 is the flat-band prediction at the magic angle, the existence of correlated insulating and superconducting phases at that angle, and their reproduction across groups and probes. What is not settled is the pairing mechanism and the full interpretation of the phase diagram. A citation would have to be written around the first set, and I now think that is premature while the picture is moving with moire TMDs and other platforms. That is why I move.

responses.point: Pearce moved from B007 to B018, asks whether Ye's share is the accuracy and many-body work or also the comb infrastructure, and asks for expert reviewers to confirm the 1e-18 claims and the inter-laboratory comparisons. He would also accept a two-name B044 of Jarillo-Herrero and MacDonald.
responses.response: I support his request for expert confirmation of the record uncertainties and the comparisons before the final ballot, since I cannot verify them from the files. On Ye's share, only the accuracy, coherence and many-body clock work is new relative to 2005, and the citation should avoid language that implies comb infrastructure. On B044, I still reject the two-name version because it drops Bistritzer, who co-authored the prediction that makes the discovery coherent. Since I am no longer proposing B044 this does not need settling now, but if it returns in a later year I would hold to the three names.

responses.point: Olsson applies the rule that a prize goes to the original experiment and not to a later and better realisation, asks whether Ye's role is decisive, and wants the citation centred on the lattice clock as a new type of instrument.
responses.response: I agree with her rule and think the pair passes it. Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and built the first strontium clock. Ye's group did more than improve the number: it showed that a many-body neutral-atom ensemble can stay coherent long enough to resolve relativistic effects across millimetres and to make the clock a many-body system, which is new physics beyond Katori's first demonstration. That is a distinct contribution, not a second discoverer repeating the first. I would record this reasoning in the discussion. I also agree with her, and with Pearce, that we should not wait for the redefinition of the second, since the accuracy is already demonstrated and reproduced.

responses.point: Danielsson finds B038 has the larger discovery content but concedes B018 has the cleaner credit, rejects waiting on B044 because the pairing mechanism is unresolved, and doubts that a second precision-measurement prize after 2005 and 2012 is justified.
responses.response: On B044 we now agree on the timing, though I still hold that an open pairing mechanism is not by itself disqualifying. On B018 I take his concern about a third precision-measurement prize seriously and have changed my view because of the distinct trapping principle and the many-atom route. I would put to him that B038, which I also think is a major result, has an attribution problem that Pearce, Mehlig and he himself describe, and three names do not settle the optical counterpart and redshift credit. Without an agreed, eligible set of individuals I cannot support it over a candidate whose credit is settled.

responses.point: Mehlig separates Katori's lattice concept from the accuracy campaign that included Lemonde, Takamoto and others, treats B018 as his first alternative, and says he could move to it if B012 looks like a sequel to 2016.
responses.response: The separation he describes is the right one for the citation, and I would draft it around the lattice concept and the demonstrated accuracy and many-body work, so that the other groups are described as reproductions and refinements rather than omitted discoverers. I think that answers part of the credit worry, though not all. On B012, I agree that the physics is mature and that the attribution is clean, but the first-order melting results and the proximity to the 2016 topological-phase-transition prize make me think the support is thinner than for B018, so I would not favour it in a final vote.

uncertainties: Whether the current record uncertainties and inter-laboratory comparisons for lattice clocks are as stated, which I cannot check and which expert reviewers should confirm.
Whether the committee accepts the magic-wavelength lattice and many-atom interrogation as a distinct discovery relative to 2005 and 2012, even with the citation wording.
Whether Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley or the Yb and Hg groups have credit claims that two names cannot fairly set aside.
Whether I am giving up B044 too early: its pairing mechanism may be understood within a few years, and the committee might regret not having recognised it.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B018 or B044. I have no known collaboration with Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Bistritzer or Jarillo-Herrero. I chaired the 2025 prize for superconducting circuits, which bears on B008 as a timing matter but is not a personal tie to any candidate. I am a theorist of electronic structure and magnetism and defer to the atomic physicists on clock metrology.
